public_rationale: Marcus forecasts that humans will be needed to fix AI-written code 'for a long time to come'. That sets no deadline. Evidence so far fits the forecast. An EASE 2026 study found human developers did about 83% of maintenance on AI-generated files, and the SWE-CI benchmark found most AI models often broke working code during long-term maintenance. But a forecast about many years ahead cannot be confirmed seven months after the post. I found no decisive event showing AI-written production software being routinely maintained without humans, which could have contradicted it early.
limitations: The evidence is early and comes from limited samples.
'Fix the mess' and 'a long time' are vague.

our_interpretation: The forecast is that human engineers will stay necessary to repair and maintain AI-written code for many years, whether or not AI ends up writing most code.
The 'AI writes most code' clause is a hedge ('may well'), not a condition. The forecast applies either way.
'For a long time to come' sets no deadline, so this is an open-horizon forecast.
criteria.support_condition: After many years (well beyond the evaluation date), credible industry or research evidence shows that human engineers are still routinely needed to fix and maintain AI-written code.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible independent evidence shows that, soon after the post, production software built mostly by AI is routinely maintained and repaired at scale without human engineers.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Long-run industry or research evidence, several years after March 2026, showing whether human engineers still routinely repair and maintain AI-written production code. Large-scale evidence of fully autonomous maintenance without humans would contradict the forecast.
